candidates.text:
A few surprising things I learned from reading about Eiichrio Oda, the creator of One Piece:

1.  He slept 3 hours a night for 15 years.

2.  He created the most successful manga of all time with more than 600 million copies in circulation.

3.  He said he would have missed his parent’s funeral because it conflicted with his work.

4.  He is extremely private. He does not allow his face to be photographed and when he appears on video he has a giant fish avatar placed on his head.

5.  When he hires a new editor the first thing he says to them is you need to be willing to die for One Piece.

6.  His editor said he might someday encounter a writer more talented than Oda but he would never meet anyone who worked harder.

7.  He doesn’t want ideas, he wants criticism.

8.  He would hand draw entire Disney animated movies to learn how to give his characters emotion.

9.  He said he only saw his family once a week because family time was too relaxing.

10.  He holds the Guinness World Record for the most copies published for the same comic book series by a single author.

11.  He is often described as a maniac due to his unbelievable work ethic and inhuman daily habits.

12.  He believes in having the least number of people possible touching the work.

13.  He says he gets his best ideas by not sleeping or eating. He says humans can only come up with truly new ideas when they reach their limit.

14.  He started working on One Piece when he was 22. He is still working on it at 51.

15.  He once spent 12 consecutive hours on the telephone discussing a single story with his editor.

16.  He has an extreme tolerance for repetition.

17.  Imagination is the organizing force of his entire life.

18.  He's a perfectionist who has repeatedly admitted that he cannot make himself work in a more efficient way, even when he desperately wants to.

19.  He never finishes before a deadline. He equates using every available minute with giving his maximum effort.

20.  He believes it’s impossible to create something great unless you do everything yourself, attend to every detail, and test it exhaustively.

21.  He believes the more experience he has the harder it is to create.

22.  He was 4 when he decided to be a manga artist. He said he wanted to avoid ever having to get a real job.

23.  He creates his work for an audience of exactly one person: himself at 15 years old.

25.  He has dedicated his entire adult life to writing a story about freedom and adventure, while accepting an extraordinarily restrictive life in order to create it.

26. To this day he does not feel successful.

--
Eiichiro Oda is a relentlessly obsessive creative genius who has devoted nearly every waking hour of his adult life to building one of the most extraordinary fictional universes ever imagined. You don't want to miss this episode:

candidates.text:
Someone shared a post on 4xR9700 Tinybox that claims to run Kimi K3 for $30k at 40tok/s with good prefill. Whenever I see something that sounds way too good to be true, I cannot resist doing my due diligence.

First, I wish them all the success and think what they are doing is amazing to make large models more accessible. However, I can’t fathom announcing a product without every single possible spec/bench to back up claim this big, and there was quite a bit missing

Since the main selling point was to offload into ‘ultra fast’ 16TB NVMe, I’ll assume they aren’t running some low bit pruned quant. If so, I cannot make the math work. Only way I can hit their number on their build is by using 1.5-2bit with god tier custom engine over Gen5 nvme

I did find benches in tinygrad's own repo, both with no SSD offload. George Hotz's K3 write-up from August, 8x MI350X, 38.65 tok/s prefill and 6.25 tok/s decode, with his own 100 tok/s target not met. K3 pull request from Oct 31, 8x MI300X, 43 tok/s prefill and 9.7 tok/s decode on hardware many tiers above R9700

Prefill wasn't in the announcement, and when asked they said they haven't tested it but it should be low. A big prompt touches nearly every expert, so roughly 1.4TB off NVMe per pass, about 6 sec on Gen5 even prefetched layer by layer. By my math that's 300-800 tok/s being very generous, 100k prompt 2-6min. They said 5000 tok/s looks doable layer by layer, would love to see it

Obviously I don’t have their box so I cannot exactly measure it, but wouldn’t need to if it was provided from the start. The lack of transparency is bit concerning personally, with such expensive hardware with huge claim

Reason I’m risking looking like an asshole to post this, which I do often anyways, is because I truly wish their claim is true. If their bench was already released and proven, my apologies x100 since I couldn’t find it. I absolutely love to be proven wrong, so I can buy one myself. 

If tinybox can truly hit their numbers without some unannounced shenanigans, I’ll be their biggest advocate for it

In August, I'd written about SEBI's proposal to simplify account opening for NRIs. Good to see that the changes have now been finalised.

For years, one of the biggest hurdles for NRIs wanting to invest in India has been account opening. While those with existing KYC could open accounts digitally, anyone abroad needing fresh KYC had to get documents attested by a notary or the Indian embassy, courier physical copies to India, and wait weeks for the account to open.

From December 3, NRIs and OCIs living in FATF-compliant countries will be able to complete digital KYC entirely from abroad. Something that took weeks can now be done in 2–3 days. 

I've always felt that making it easier for NRIs to invest is one of the simplest ways to attract more long-term capital into India. Many of them already want to invest here, but the process has been complicated.

At @zerodha, we've been able to simplify several things for NRIs over the last year, but account opening has remained one of the biggest challenges.

With this change, there's no reason why you, as an NRI, should go elsewhere to trade and invest 🙂

candidates.text:
everything i know about thumbnails, in 12 lines.

1. the eye scans a thumbnail in about 0.02 seconds. it moves in a z from top left to bottom right, so put your hook top left, and your proof bottom right.

2. use three elements at most, like a face, some text and one object. three is the most the brain can read instantly.

3. make one element clearly the main focus. everything else should support it, so the eye knows where to land.

4. add a twist the title doesn't say. a thumbnail that only repeats the title gives no reason to click.

5. avoid red, white and black as your main colours. youtube's own page uses them, so your thumbnail blends in.

6. put your most intense colour on the twist. the twist is what makes people curious, so it should catch the eye first.

7. break your niche's usual look on exactly one element. break one and it's memorable. break all of them and nobody recognises what it is.

8. turn it black and white before you publish. if you can't still tell what matters most, the contrast is too weak.

9. show the result the viewer wants as a picture. the eye reads the thumbnail before the title, so the picture has to carry the promise.

10. light your face from one side. look for a small triangle of shadow beside your nose. phones default to flat light, so flat light looks amateur.

11. pose for the thumbnail on set. frames pulled from your footage are usually blurry, badly lit or caught mid word.

12. make your face show the feeling the title promises. your expression tells the viewer how the video will feel.

I heard that a lot of new dads don't really connect with their newborn until the baby starts smiling back at them, perhaps at 6 or 9 or 12 months

That has not been my experience. And I think I know why

I told a friend whose wife is pregnant (he also likes cats): having a baby is like having a cat, but it’s YOUR cat that your wife made in her belly for 9 or 10 months

You feed the baby, you pet and snuggle the baby, you dress the baby, you change the baby. The baby sleeps a lot and eats very often

If you like animals and pets, you’ll probably like having a newborn. It’s really cool and fun to have a living, breathing thing in the house that you take care of

A lot of the talk online is about how a dad's experience is so different from the mom’s because the mom bonds ASAP. But that hasn’t been true for me and I think a lot of that is because I like animals
